prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "AMAZON COM INC" (ticker AMZN). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Amazon has most Rule Breaker traits: it leads big trends in cloud, AI and online retail, it is run by a strong team, and many people see it as a strong brand. Its shares rose 19.5% over the past 52 weeks, about the same as the S&P 500's 20.4% total return, so its market lead is not clear-cut. Critics who call it overvalued, a trait Gardner sees as a good sign, are less common now that it trades at 20.8 times trailing earnings.
summaries.buffett: Amazon has a wide moat, a durable franchise and capable management, which Buffett values, but its economics have shifted. AI data-centre capital spending pushed trailing free cash flow to an outflow of $7.6B as of Q2 2026, and it has never paid a dividend, so owner earnings are hard to pin down today. The price of $258.58 does not offer the clear discount to intrinsic value that Buffett prefers.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire Amazon's flywheel of scale, low prices and a culture of frugality and long-term thinking, and he would see it as a business with very few ways to fail outright. The open questions are whether more than $150B a year of AI capex will earn good returns and how antitrust rules will treat it. It fits his 'great business at a fair price' idea better than his 'obviously cheap' one.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms Amazon is a large fast grower turning into a stalwart, with a simple story: AWS, advertising and Prime drive profit growth. Its forward P/E of 27.6 and PEG of 1.33 (StockAnalysis) are above Lynch's ideal of a P/E at or below the growth rate, the share count is still rising, and Wall Street follows it heavily. A Lynch investor would find it a sound business, though not an overlooked bargain.
summaries.fisher: Amazon fits Fisher's 15 points well: it keeps building new products (Bedrock, Trainium chips, Alexa+, Amazon Leo, Zoox), it is excellent at selling and distribution, and its management puts long-term growth ahead of quarterly profit. Fisher would weigh up the lower GAAP margins of its retail arm and how candid management is about the payback on AI spending. Overall it is close to the long-term growth company Fisher sought.
summaries.graham: Amazon fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests. It has never paid a dividend, it lost $2.7B in 2022, and its P/E (20.8) times its P/B (5.05) is about 105, far above Graham's limit of 22.5. Its size and strong finances meet only his first criteria.
summaries.thiel: Amazon answers most of Thiel's seven questions well: it has a durable monopoly-like position in US e-commerce logistics and a strong number-one spot in cloud, plus excellent distribution and a great team. Thiel would question whether AWS's technology is still 10 times better now that Microsoft and Google compete closely in AI cloud. Amazon began by dominating a small niche (online books) and expanded from there, the path Thiel describes.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's approach of backing durable AI-era compounders while insisting on cost discipline fits Amazon. It is a top beneficiary of AI computing, and Andy Jassy has cut management layers and lifted margins. The concern Gerstner would raise is capital efficiency, since free cash flow has turned negative because of capex. The valuation, at a forward P/E of 27.6, is reasonable for its growth rather than cheap.
summaries.druckenmiller: For Druckenmiller the setup is mixed. Operating income rose 43% in Q2 2026 and AWS growth sped up to 37%, but the shares only matched the market over the last year and capex is consuming cash. He would want to see earnings revisions and AWS momentum turn into a clear price trend before making a large bet.
summaries.smith: Amazon does not fully meet Terry Smith's tests. Its ROIC of about 12% (StockAnalysis) is moderate, its 50.8% gross margin is moderate, and free cash flow is negative, while Fundsmith wants high returns, high margins and strong cash conversion. It qualifies as a good company with a long runway, but its current cash generation falls short of his 'good company' standard.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Amazon ranks poorly. EV/EBIT is about 31 (StockAnalysis), an earnings yield of roughly 3%, and its return on capital is only moderate. A Greenblatt screen would not pick it today.
summaries.akre: On Akre's three-legged stool, Amazon has an excellent business and capable, owner-minded management (Bezos is still a large holder), and it has a long runway to reinvest. The weak leg today is reinvestment returns, because heavy AI capex has pushed free cash flow negative and ROIC is only about 12%. It is a partial fit until that spending proves its returns.
summaries.pabrai: Amazon is not a Dhandho bet. It is not a distressed, simple business priced for a heads-I-win outcome, and at $258.58 with a forward P/E of 27.6 the market already expects success. Pabrai would like its low risk of permanent loss, but he would find no large mispricing.
summaries.wood: Amazon fits ARK's view of convergent innovation well: it combines AI (Bedrock, Trainium, Anthropic partnership), robotics (over 1 million warehouse robots), autonomous mobility (Zoox) and satellite internet (Amazon Leo). Its size limits how many times its market value can multiply, and that matters to ARK, which seeks five-year compounding. It is a broad platform holding rather than a pure disruptive play.
summaries.ackman: Amazon meets several of Pershing Square's criteria: a simple, predictable, dominant business with high barriers to entry and a long growth runway. It falls short on free cash flow generation today and is exposed to capex cycles, antitrust and labour issues. Ackman would also want a larger margin of safety than the current price offers.
summaries.sleep: Amazon is the textbook Nick Sleep business: Nomad held it as the clearest case of 'scale economies shared', passing savings from its growing size back to customers through low prices and free shipping. That model is intact, with Prime, the regional delivery network and AWS price cuts. The question Sleep would ask is whether AI capex reinforces that flywheel or dilutes it.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets with a product that solves a big problem, and Amazon has several: retail convenience, cloud computing and AI infrastructure. As a mature company of about $2.8T it is far from Sequoia's early-stage focus, but its markets and customer problems are the kind Valentine favoured.

momentum.evidence: AMZN closed at $258.58 on 13 October 2026, up 19.5% over 52 weeks, roughly level with the S&P 500 ETF SPY's 20.4% total return, so it rose solidly but did not beat the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Andy Jassy, who built AWS, runs the company and founder Jeff Bezos remains executive chair, and Amazon has partnerships with leading AI developers such as Anthropic.

g6.evidence: Some commentators question the return on its AI capex, but at 20.8 times trailing earnings, with 60 analysts rating it a Strong Buy (StockAnalysis), it is not widely called overvalued.

simple.evidence: Its main businesses (online store, marketplace fees, AWS cloud, advertising, Prime subscriptions) are well disclosed by segment and easy for a generalist to follow.

b2.evidence: Net sales grew every year from $386B in 2020 to about $717B in 2025, but profits swung to a net loss of $2.7B in 2022.

integrity.evidence: Amazon's shareholder letters are candid and pay is mostly in long-term stock, but it pays no dividend, the share count is still rising (+0.88% year on year), and it faces FTC antitrust litigation.

b6.evidence: Amazon pursues bets of its own, such as Trainium chips, Amazon Leo and Zoox, rather than copying peers, but it is entering many adjacent markets at once.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 12% and ROE about 31% (StockAnalysis); returns are boosted by AWS but diluted by low-margin retail, and long-term debt reached $128.9B in June 2026.

fcf.evidence: Operating cash flow was $161.4B over the trailing twelve months to Q2 2026, but heavy capex turned free cash flow into an outflow of $7.6B.

b10.evidence: Amazon has kept all its earnings since its 1997 IPO and has turned that retained capital into AWS, advertising and logistics businesses now worth about $2.8T in market value.

safety.evidence: At $258.58 the stock trades at 20.8 times trailing earnings, inflated by Anthropic stake gains, and 27.6 times forward earnings, so the price has no conservative margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 27.6 and PEG of 1.33 (StockAnalysis) are reasonable for 20% revenue growth in Q2 2026, but the negative free cash flow makes the stock harder to value.

mu5.evidence: With diversified profit streams in AWS, advertising, subscriptions and retail, and $123B of cash, there are few ways for Amazon to fail outright; the main risks are regulation and AI overinvestment.

reinvest.evidence: AWS earned $16.6B of operating income on $42.2B of revenue in Q2 2026 while growing 37%, which shows it can reinvest heavily at attractive returns.

ly2.evidence: Amazon is a large fast grower or stalwart with a simple story: AWS, advertising and Prime drive rising profits on top of the retail base.

ly3.evidence: Its PEG ratio is 1.33 (StockAnalysis), so the P/E is somewhat above the expected earnings growth rate.

runway.evidence: Consensus expects revenue to reach about $1.25T by 2030 (TickFlow), driven by AI cloud, advertising, international retail, healthcare and satellite internet.

ly7.evidence: The share count rose 0.88% year on year, and founder Jeff Bezos has been a regular seller under pre-arranged trading plans.

ly8.evidence: Amazon is one of the most widely covered stocks, with 60 analysts (StockAnalysis), and it sits in high-profile sectors.

fi2.evidence: As retail matures Amazon keeps launching new lines, including Bedrock and Trainium for AI, Alexa+, Amazon Leo satellite internet and Zoox robotaxis.

fi3.evidence: Its heavy technology spending produced AWS, custom Graviton and Trainium chips and the logistics robotics that lowered its cost to serve.

fi4.evidence: Amazon is the default US online shopping destination, and its advertising business grew 26% year on year in Q2 2026.

longterm.evidence: Since Bezos's 1997 letter, Amazon has put long-term free cash flow and market leadership ahead of short-term earnings, as its current AI capex shows.

gr1.evidence: Net sales were about $717B in 2025, among the largest of any company in the world.

ni10.evidence: Amazon reported a net loss of $2.7B in 2022, so it was not profitable in each of the last ten years.

gr4.evidence: Amazon has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.25 in 2015 (about $0.06 adjusted for the 2022 20-for-1 split) to $7.17 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: Average EPS for 2023-2025 was about $5.20 ($2.90, $5.53, $7.17), so $258.58 is about 50 times average earnings, far above 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of 20.8 times P/B of 5.05 (StockAnalysis) is about 105, far above Graham's 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its logistics network and AWS's breadth are hard to copy, but they are not 10 times better than Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud or Walmart in every area.

timing.evidence: AI workloads are speeding up cloud demand, and AWS growth accelerated to 37% year on year in Q2 2026.

th3.evidence: Amazon started by dominating online book sales in 1995 and expanded step by step into general retail, a marketplace, cloud and advertising.

team.evidence: Founder Jeff Bezos is executive chair, and CEO Andy Jassy founded and built AWS, the largest cloud platform.

th5.evidence: Prime membership, the marketplace's traffic and AWS's enterprise sales force give Amazon unmatched distribution to consumers and businesses.

durable.evidence: Its delivery network, Prime base and hyperscale cloud are hard to replicate, though AI shopping agents and AI-cloud rivals are real long-term threats.

th7.evidence: AWS in 2006 was a unique insight, but today's AI cloud opportunity is pursued equally by Microsoft, Google and Oracle.

trend.evidence: AWS is the largest cloud provider with about 28% share (Synergy, Q1 2026) and is a leading beneficiary of AI computing, as are its Trainium chips.

dr1.evidence: Q2 2026 operating income rose 43% to $27.5B, AWS growth accelerated to 37%, and consensus FY2026 revenue stands at $828.5B, about 16% growth (StockAnalysis).

dr2.evidence: As new AI data centres come online, AWS revenue and margins could rise and capex intensity could ease, but how quickly this happens is uncertain.

dr4.evidence: Amazon is less rate-sensitive than most companies thanks to $123B of cash, but rising debt for AI capex and dependence on consumer spending tie it to the economy.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on 29 October 2026, new AWS capacity coming online, Anthropic stake gains and Amazon Leo's commercial launch could all drive results.

dr7.evidence: The business quality supports a large position, but negative free cash flow and capex uncertainty argue against maximum concentration now.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 50.8% (StockAnalysis), boosted by AWS, advertising and services but held down by first-party retail.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow is negative (an outflow of $7.6B), so the free-cash-flow yield is below zero.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 31 (EV about $2.92T, StockAnalysis), an earnings yield of about 3%.

pa2.evidence: The negative free cash flow comes from a temporary AI capex build-out rather than a broken business, but the stock is not depressed.

pa4.evidence: With dominant franchises, $161.4B of trailing operating cash flow and $123B of cash, the risk of permanent capital loss is small.

wo1.evidence: Amazon is a leader in AI infrastructure (AWS, Trainium, Bedrock) and in robotics, with over 1 million warehouse robots.

wo2.evidence: Its own chips and robotics lower unit costs as volumes grow, but costs are not falling at the steep learning-curve rates ARK looks for.

wo3.evidence: It combines AI, robotics, autonomous vehicles (Zoox) and satellite internet (Amazon Leo) on one platform.

wo4.evidence: AI cloud and new businesses could greatly expand its market, but at about $717B of sales its total addressable market is unlikely to grow many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: It is not a commodity producer, but energy costs for data centres, fuel for delivery and consumer demand affect its results.

ns1.evidence: Amazon passes scale savings to customers through low prices, free Prime shipping and periodic AWS price cuts, which makes it harder to compete with.

ns4.evidence: Its logistics and cloud lead are likely to persist, but AI competition and agent-driven shopping make a stronger position in 10-20 years probable rather than certain.

va2.evidence: It solves large, painful problems: getting goods quickly and cheaply, and letting firms run computing and AI without building data centres.
